prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints and asset prices interact to amplify and propagate shocks, and thereby explaining credit cycles

statement.case_for:
My configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single part for B011 with Kiyotaki and Moore. After the exchange I hold it with somewhat less confidence than in the opening, for the reasons below. Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) identify one precise mechanism. Borrowing limits depend on collateral values, and collateral values depend on borrowing. That feedback makes small, temporary shocks large and persistent. From a corporate-finance and financial-contracting standpoint, the idea is the macro counterpart of how real lenders contract with firms: they lend against pledgeable assets, not against future income. The mechanism has been used for nearly three decades in macro-finance and in policy models. It is a clean two-author origin, so the credit needs no division. The exchange confirmed that the attribution case is strong. All six B011 supporters now name the same two people, and the competing objections concern the 2022 overlap and empirical identification, not whether the credit is correct. I weigh the identification objection seriously. I do not think it is decisive, because the prize can recognise a mechanism whose implications have been examined in many settings. I recall firm-level work linking investment and borrowing to collateral values, but I have not verified it here. The six-vote tally is narrow and includes the chair and a frequent co-author of the chair. I therefore treat it as no evidence of merit.

Proposed wording for the chair's question on what is not honoured: the citation names the collateral-price feedback mechanism only. It does not honour the bank-run and bank-information literature recognised in 2022, nor the borrower-net-worth financial-accelerator strand and its quantitative policy models. If the committee wanted that strand recognised, it would need its own argued citation.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises. I think the mechanism is distinct, but a committee could still read the area as recently honoured. The second reservation is identification. The collateral channel is better established as a framework and modelling building block than as a measured magnitude, and the colleagues who prefer B005 are right that heterogeneous-firm selection has been tested more directly on micro data. Excluding Gertler and Gilchrist leaves out the strand that carried financial frictions into quantitative policy models. That is a real cost to completeness, even if it is the right cost for attribution. Finally, my own field is adjacent. Financial contracting and collateral are close to my research, so I may overrate a mechanism that speaks to questions I care about. B005 is a serious competitor on maturity and breadth of confirmation, and if the committee judged the 2022 overlap decisive against B011, B005 is where I would go.

responses.point: Friberg prefers B005. He argues that Melitz (2003) and the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple work are general, confirmed on firm-level data in many countries, and cleanly attributable to two people. He would anchor the citation on selection and reallocation across firms, not claim the empirical discovery of exporter heterogeneity, and he would not widen to Redding or the empirical contributors.
responses.response: I accept the directness-of-testing point. B005 beats B011 on that dimension, and I do not wave it away. My difference is on attribution. Your own account concedes that Bernard and Jensen documented the exporter facts, that Eaton-Kortum is a distinct strand, and that Helpman's marginal credit has to be separated from Krugman's 2008 prize. All of that can be managed by wording, as you say. But it still needs more explanation than the B011 citation, which rests on one two-author paper. The chair asked whether a Melitz-centred credit would be more defensible. I do not think I can answer that without a full account of Helpman's independent contribution, and it is a one-name award with a different scientific profile. I would support B005 with your wording if the committee found the credit lines clean. For me it remains the first alternative, and the two cases are close.

responses.point: Fredriksson moved from B019 to B005. She describes B011 as conceptually foundational but weakly identified, and she says the 2022 overlap weighs more heavily with her than the B011 supporters allow.
responses.response: I answer the chair's question to B005 supporters in part through your objection. On overlap, the 2022 citation concerned banks, bank runs and the study of financial crises. The Kiyotaki-Moore mechanism concerns collateral values and dynamic amplification, and it applies equally to non-bank borrowers such as firms. I would keep the overlap as a wording and framing issue, not a ground for demotion. On identification I concede more. A model that is mainly validated as a reusable building block is a different kind of achievement from one with decades of micro-data testing. The committee should say so explicitly, and I would not describe the crisis as confirmation of the mechanism. If you judge that a prize for a mechanism of this kind should wait for stronger direct evidence, I understand the position. I read the prize as covering mechanisms with demonstrated explanatory reach, and I think B011 meets that.

responses.point: Boppart now puts B005 first and B011 as his first alternative. He says the choice is closer than his opening ranks suggested, that the Kiyotaki-Moore overlap concerns the broader accelerator lineage more than the mechanism, and that he would not add a third name to B011.
responses.response: This is the clearest answer to the chair's question on whether B005 supporters could accept a two-name B011. You say you could, with attribution care and a narrow citation, and I agree that the narrow wording above does that work. On B001, you moved away from Mian-Sufi because of recency and the unsettled weight of credit supply. I share that reading, and for the same reason I do not use B001 to argue for B011. I treat Kiyotaki-Moore as the general mechanism and Mian-Sufi as an identified application, not as a rival. Where we still differ is the weight on direct firm-level evidence. You put it first. I put it second to the cleanness of a single-paper origin. I do not think the committee can settle this by argument alone, and the private vote will.

responses.point: Teorell prefers B012. He has moved toward treating B011 as a serious alternative after Hassler's argument on the 2022 prize. He concedes that identification of constitutional and electoral-rule effects is the weakest part of the case and that the field is dispersed across many contributors.
responses.response: I appreciate that you re-examined the 2022 overlap, and I think your revised reading is right. On B012, your concession on identification and dispersion is the reason I keep it as an alternative and not my preferred part. A citation anchored on the formal framework and the later state-capacity work, which you propose, is the defensible version. I would add that it does not answer how the committee draws a three-name boundary in a dispersed field. B011 draws it at one paper. The chair asked which alternative you would support in a single-part prize if B012 cannot reach six votes. I would be interested in your answer, because I suspect the realistic choice is between B011 and B005. I note your point that recent attention to the institutions theme should not count against a distinct mechanism, and I agree with it as a matter of principle.

responses.point: Hassler, as chair, prefers B011 with Kiyotaki and Moore only. He keeps B005 as the alternative and says the B005 citation is harder to draw cleanly because of the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum attribution and the Krugman overlap. He asks the committee to discuss the Helpman-Melitz boundary if it moves toward B005.
responses.response: I agree with the attribution comparison, and I also agree with the caution in your chair observation. The six-vote lead is narrow, and both of us, together with Krusell, are on the B011 side. For that reason I would not let the count settle anything. On the practical question of a two-part pairing, I cannot construct one under the three-person cap that does not damage attribution. B011 plus B005 would be four names, and dropping one on either side would weaken a clean credit. I therefore take a single part as the working assumption for the vote.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads the 2022 prize as covering collateral-based amplification. I think the mechanism is distinct, but the answer depends on citation wording and on how the committee weighs recent recognition.

How much indirect empirical identification of the collateral channel should count against a foundational mechanism, relative to the direct firm-level testing of B005. I have not independently verified the strength of the firm-level evidence on collateral values.

Whether excluding Gertler and Gilchrist undercredits the quantitative financial-accelerator strand. I would not object if the committee decided otherwise, but I have not seen an argument that separates his contribution from the work recognised in 2022.

Whether the Helpman-Melitz credit for B005 can be drawn cleanly given Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, the 2008 prize and Helpman's separate B020 entry. If it can, B005 would be a close competitor and might be preferable.

Whether my own field adjacency to financial contracting leads me to overweight B011. These assessments rest on general knowledge and the supplied committee texts, not on independently verified sources.
statement.conflict_note: No co-authorship or institutional tie to Kiyotaki, Moore, Helpman, Melitz, Persson, Tabellini or Besley is shown in my supplied profile. Disclosures follow. (1) Field adjacency: my research on financial contracting and collateralised borrowing is close to B011. I chaired the committee for the 2016 contract-theory prize and gave that presentation speech, which may incline me toward contracting-related work, and a collectively drafted speech does not establish a voting preference. John Moore is known for contract-theory work outside the credited 1997 mechanism, and I do not credit that work here. (2) Fredriksson and Teorell refer to a remark of mine about Torsten Persson's past committee role (B012). That remark is not in my round-1 file, so I cannot reproduce or rely on it. My profile shows no personal tie to Persson. I disclose that B012 includes a former committee member, that I ranked B012 third and list it as an alternative, and that I leave the question unadjudicated. (3) I have long committee overlap with Hassler, Krusell, Ellingsen and Svensson, and I am Vice President of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences. These are collegial and institutional relationships, not ties to any candidate. Conflicts are disclosed here and not adjudicated.
